title: not just a party
hookLine: a thirteen-year-old, an ancient scroll, then the DJ: which part is the real thing?
tomorrow: an argument for the sake of heaven

cards: A thirteen-year-old in a suit that doesn't quite fit, or a dress picked out months ago, stands in front of everyone they know and chants from a handwritten scroll, in Hebrew they've practiced for a year.
Then comes the party: the DJ, the candy bar, the chair lifted into the air. So which part was the real thing? Neither one, it turns out, makes it happen.

teach.h: SON OR DAUGHTER OF THE COMMANDMENT.
teach.b: Bar mitzvah means son of the commandment. Bat mitzvah, daughter of the commandment. A mitzvah is one of the things the Torah asks a person to do, and in everyday talk it's also a good deed: that was a real mitzvah.
Here's the twist. You don't have a bar or bat mitzvah.

In traditional Jewish law it happens on its own, on a birthday: thirteen for boys, twelve for girls, and many communities mark both at thirteen. Ceremony or no ceremony, party or no party, the day comes.

An old teaching lays out a life by ages: five for starting scripture, ten for the rabbis' teachings, thirteen for the commandments. Until then, the responsibility sat with your parents. From that birthday on, it's yours.
So the ceremony isn't what makes it happen.

teach.h: SHOWN IN PUBLIC, THEN A MEAL.
teach.b: It's the first time it's shown in public: called up to read from the Torah, often with a short talk about what that week's reading means to you. And the party? Celebrating a mitzvah with a festive meal is a tradition too.
The DJ is newer. Some people take it up as adults, at thirty or sixty or eighty. There's no deadline.
And if your own bar or bat mitzvah was the last time you really took part, you're in very good company. Picking it up again years later isn't starting over. It's carrying on.

how: A Jewish boy becomes bar mitzvah at thirteen and a girl bat mitzvah at twelve in traditional law (thirteen in many communities); many mark it by being called up to read from the Torah, often chanting the week's portion and giving a short talk, followed by a festive meal, and some adults celebrate it later in life.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: think back to being twelve or thirteen. Second breath: one thing you're responsible for now that you weren't then.
Third breath: let it be yours, without the weight. Just yours.

wordCard.voice: Mitzvah. A commandment, a good deed, and at a bar or bat mitzvah, a responsibility that becomes yours. Sixth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a commandment. in everyday talk, a good deed.

carryVoice: Your line: it's yours now. The day comes on its own; the ceremony just says so out loud. Day six.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 5:21 (five for scripture, ten for Mishnah, thirteen for the commandments)

Genesis Rabbah 63:10 (a father's responsibility until thirteen)
